  1. Routing & type-safe DI
  2. ESLint rules

ESLint rules#

The rule set is not decoration: several checks in this documentation only work because a rule generated or maintained the code they read. Others enforce the architecture — no hidden runtime dependencies or direct transport calls — and most of them autofix.

Install them once when you set up routing and type-safe DI. Then lean on the quick fixes rather than writing the boilerplate by hand.

An ESLint error is not a compile error

A missing autofix does not break the build. If you skip the quick fix after changing route metadata, the same-file DI proof or exhaustiveness check may be missing. Run eslint --fix in CI so those proofs stay armed.

The plugin is exposed from @craft-ts/dev-tools/eslint-rules.

Route app-local links through Craft#

craft-ts/prefer-craft-router-link is enabled at error in the recommended and Effect presets, including generated apps. The demo application's client source enables the same rule explicitly. It rejects app-relative href values on Craft anchors so the router can capture and replay route changes.

Before — this native anchor reloads the document instead of using the app router:

ts
// ❌ app-local destination
a('hero-shop', { href: '/catalogue' }, 'Découvrir la boutique');

After — name the Craft route and let CraftRouterLink handle the navigation:

ts
a('hero-shop', {}, 'Découvrir la boutique').pipe(
  CraftRouterLink({ to: 'catalogue' }),
);

External destinations remain native links:

ts
a(
  'documentation',
  { href: 'https://example.com/guide', target: '_blank' },
  'Documentation',
);

Static app-relative paths such as '/catalogue', 'catalogue', './catalogue' and '../catalogue' are rejected. Absolute URLs, protocol-relative URLs, fragment links, downloads, and _blank links are allowed. A dynamic href is reported because ESLint cannot tell whether it points inside or outside the app; mark a deliberately native URL with data-navigation: 'external'.

There is no autofix: the author must map the destination to a declared Craft route (including any route parameters). Use CraftRouterLink for anchor navigation and CraftRouter.navigate(...) for navigation initiated by a button or another action.

Keep route state in Craft routing#

craft-ts/no-manual-craft-routing is enabled at error in the recommended and Effect presets, including generated apps. It catches browser location reads of hash and pathname, hand-parsed hash route checks, same-app writes to location.hash or location.href, location.assign(...) / replace(...) calls to app paths, URL-bearing history.pushState / replaceState calls, and subscriptions to popstate or hashchange. These patterns implement route matching, navigation, or history tracking outside provideCraftRouter and CraftRouterOutlet.

Before — the service parses the route and changes it by editing browser history:

ts
const sessionId = /^#\/sessions\/([^/]+)$/.exec(location.hash)?.[1];
history.pushState({}, '', `#/sessions/${nextSessionId}`);

After — declare the path parameter with the route, then use Craft's typed route helpers and navigation API:

ts
// In the route declaration:
{
  path: 'sessions/:sessionId',
  pathParams: { sessionId: sessionIdPathParam },
  // Route providers expose SessionIdParams to the page's services.
}

// In a routed service:
const sessionId = yield* SessionIdParams();
const router = yield* CraftRouter();
yield* router.navigate({
  to: 'sessions/:sessionId',
  params: { sessionId: nextSessionId },
});

The rule has no autofix: choosing a route and mapping parsed values to its typed path or query parameters requires understanding the feature. It leaves fragment links and ordinary location.search reads alone. Browser URL work for a separate protocol (such as a worker or iframe) should remain behind that protocol's boundary, rather than deciding which app page is active.

craft-ts/prefer-craft-route-over-page-state adds a softer warning at warn in the recommended and Effect presets. A string-valued state('page', ...), state('currentPage', ...), state('activePage', ...), or state('routePage', ...) can duplicate the route table by storing which page the URL already selects.

Before — local state selects which routed page is visible:

ts
const page = yield * state('page', 'sessions');

After — declare both pages in craftRoutes and let the router activate one in CraftRouterOutlet():

ts
import { loadCraftComponent } from '@craft-ts/component';
import { CraftRouterOutlet, craftRoute, craftRoutes } from '@craft-ts/core';

export const { appRoutes } = craftRoutes('app', [
  craftRoute('sessions', {
    ...loadCraftComponent(({ withRetry }) =>
      withRetry(import('./sessions-page')).then(
        (module) => module.SessionsPage,
      ),
    ),
  }),
  craftRoute('sessions/:sessionId', {
    ...loadCraftComponent(({ withRetry }) =>
      withRetry(import('./replay-page')).then((module) => module.ReplayPage),
    ),
  }),
]);

// In the application shell's template:
main(CraftRouterOutlet());

This is a review warning, not an error: names such as page can also mean pagination or page-local UI state. Keep those states when they do not choose the active route. The warning has no autofix.

Use Craft state and computed values#

craft-ts/no-direct-craft-reactivity is enabled at error in the recommended and Effect presets, including generated apps. It rejects imports of the low-level craftSignal and ɵcomputed factories from @craft-ts/core. They produce signal-shaped values without the lifecycle, naming, composition, and runtime tracking provided by Craft primitives.

Before — aliasing the factories makes them look like general purpose signals:

ts
import { ɵcomputed as computed, craftSignal as signal } from '@craft-ts/core';

const count = signal(0);
const doubled = computed(() => count() * 2);

After — declare writable values with state and derived values with craftComputed inside a Craft service:

ts
import { craftComputed, craftService, state } from '@craft-ts/core';

const { Counter } = craftService(
  { name: 'Counter', providedIn: 'global' },
  function* () {
    const count = yield* state('count', 0, ({ update }) => ({
      increment: () => update((value) => value + 1),
    }));
    yield* craftComputed('doubled', function* () {
      return (yield* count()) * 2;
    });
  },
);

There is no autofix: the author must choose the owning service and its scope, then expose the state methods and computed values that consumers need.

craft-ts/prefer-craft-computed-for-reactive-array-length is enabled at error in the recommended preset, including generated apps. It keeps array-derived presentation state inside the service that owns the reactive array.

Before — a template decides whether a reactive list is empty or counts its items:

ts
hidden: function* () {
  return (yield* (yield* ReplayResumesViewModel()).messages()).length === 0;
},
heading: function* () {
  return plural(
    (yield* (yield* ReplayResumesViewModel()).derived()).length,
    'session',
  );
},

After — expose the boolean or count with craftComputed in the service, then read that scalar in the template:

ts
const hasNoMessages = yield* craftComputed('hasNoMessages', function* () {
  return (yield* messages()).length === 0;
});
const derivedSessionCount = yield* craftComputed(
  'derivedSessionCount',
  function* () {
    return (yield* derived()).length;
  },
);

hidden: function* () {
  return yield* (yield* ReplayResumesViewModel()).hasNoMessages();
},
heading: function* () {
  return plural(
    yield* (yield* ReplayResumesViewModel()).derivedSessionCount(),
    'session',
  );
},

There is no autofix because the owning service must choose the scalar API and its name. Reading .length inside that service's craftComputed remains valid.

craft-ts/no-mutable-craft-service-closure-state is enabled at error in the recommended and Effect presets, including generated apps. It rejects a local service variable that a craftExpose(...) callback assigns, increments, or mutates through a property. Those values persist between calls, but ordinary JavaScript closures hide their updates from Craft's state graph.

Before — exposed actions mutate closure variables imperatively:

ts
let watching: Lookup | undefined;
let pollRun = 0;

yield *
  craftExpose('watch', (lookup: Lookup) => {
    watching = lookup;
    pollRun += 1;
  });

After — declare the values with state() and make updates named insertions:

ts
const watcher =
  yield *
  state(
    'watcher',
    { lookup: undefined as Lookup | undefined, run: 0 },
    ({ update }) => ({
      start: (lookup: Lookup) =>
        update((current) => ({ lookup, run: current.run + 1 })),
      stop: () =>
        update((current) => ({ lookup: undefined, run: current.run + 1 })),
    }),
  );

// The service exposes these insertions as watcher.start and watcher.stop.

Use the state's reactive value when scheduled work needs to read the current watch target or generation. The rule has no autofix because the state shape and its insertion API depend on the service's behavior. It reports direct writes inside exposed callbacks; writes delegated to helper functions are outside its static analysis.

Only provable reads go inside a craftComputed#

craft-ts/no-craft-computed-side-effects and craft-ts/prefer-computed-local-dependency are both enabled at error in the recommended preset, including generated apps, and they share one predicate: a call is accepted inside a computed only when its type proves it is a read. prefer-computed-local-dependency asks to move a dependency into the computed that uses it only when that predicate accepts it there, so the two rules never ask for opposite things.

The evidence the predicate accepts:

  • a reactive Craft read (state, craftComputed, a query reader, a component input, a CraftServiceInput), settled(...) and syncEffect(...);

  • the synchronous core capabilities CraftRouter() and CraftGlobalError();

  • an @craft-ts/i18n translator built by runtime.bind(dependency), and the reader it returns, when its type proves that the bound dependency is a reactive Craft read and that the message resolves no service (no DI-aware token).

Resolving any other service — abstract or concrete, by Service() or by a shortcut such as Store.count() — is not proven: the resolution can instantiate the implementation inside the computation, with transitive dependencies such as a craftEffect or a write, and neither an abstract contract nor a service's dependency map proves that it has none.

Before — rejected by no-craft-computed-side-effects, because HostLocale() resolves a service inside the computation:

ts
export const { Greeting, provideGreeting } = craftService(
  { name: 'Greeting', providedIn: 'toProvide' },
  function* () {
    const name = yield* state('name', 'Ada');
    yield* craftComputed('greeting', function* () {
      const locale = yield* HostLocale(); // ❌ resolves a service
      return `${locale}: ${yield* name()}`;
    });
  },
);

After — the service body resolves HostLocale() once and the computed reads the value. prefer-computed-local-dependency accepts this form: it does not ask to move a dependency that the computed rule cannot prove pure.

ts
export const { Greeting, provideGreeting } = craftService(
  { name: 'Greeting', providedIn: 'toProvide' },
  function* () {
    const name = yield* state('name', 'Ada');
    const locale = yield* HostLocale();
    yield* craftComputed('greeting', function* () {
      return `${locale}: ${yield* name()}`;
    });
  },
);

A translation read in a computed is accepted when the translator is bound to a reactive read:

ts
const language = yield* state('language', 'en');
const t = runtime.bind(language);
const lines = yield* state('lines', [1, 2, 3]);
yield* craftComputed('summary', function* () {
  return yield* t('items', { count: (yield* lines()).length })(); // ✅
});

The same reader is rejected when bind received a generator that is not a reactive Craft read (bind it to the state that holds the locale), or when the message uses a DI-aware token: rendering it resolves that token's service, so read the translation in a template binding instead. Neither rule has an autofix; the diagnostic names the proof that is missing.

Imported state and action references#

craft-ts/no-imported-state-actions is enabled at error in the recommended and Effect presets. An imported mutable reference remains outside the current component or service's dependency graph, even when used from a Craft callback. Resolve its owner with yield* in the Craft factory and use the yielded value, or pass the needed capability to a standalone helper as an explicit input.

Before — a helper closes over state and resource references imported from a different module:

ts
import { status, archive } from './shared-state';

export function removeSession(id: string) {
  status.set('Suppression…');
  archive.deleteSession.mutate(id);
}

After — pass the required actions from the caller's DI scope:

ts
type RemoveSessionActions = {
  status: { set(value: string): void };
  deleteSession: { mutate(id: string): unknown };
};

export function removeSession(actions: RemoveSessionActions, id: string) {
  actions.status.set('Suppression…');
  actions.deleteSession.mutate(id);
}

The caller resolves status and archive through its Craft service or component dependencies, then passes only the capabilities this helper needs. Inside a service, use the yielded API directly. There is no autofix because the right owner and lifetime are application decisions.

Keep state writes yieldable#

craft-ts/no-state-facade rejects a custom callable type that combines a synchronous state reader with mutation methods such as set or update. That shape hides the state's Craft owner and makes writes look like ordinary signal mutations. ESLint cannot choose the correct owner or execution boundary, so there is no automatic fix; replace the facade manually.

Before — rejected: a local facade invents a second state API:

ts
type StateFacade<T> = (() => T) & {
  set(value: T): void;
  update(change: (current: T) => T): void;
};

After — expose insertion methods from state(...) and yield their writes:

ts
const counter =
  yield *
  state('counter', 0, ({ set, update }) => ({
    set,
    update,
  }));

yield * counter.set(1);
yield * counter.update((value) => value + 1);

For a synchronous platform callback, send one intent event and let the owning state react with on$(); do not publish a mutable state facade to the rest of the feature. craft-ts/no-imported-state-actions separately rejects mutation calls made directly on imported bindings.

Declare recurring resource triggers as streams#

craft-ts/no-recursive-craft-schedule reports a scheduled callback that passes itself back to schedule(...). That pattern creates an imperative recurring loop: the callback owns both the work and the decision to run again. When the recurrence triggers a query, mutation, or asyncProcess, declare its cadence as a stream and pass that stream as the resource's method instead.

Before — the callback manually schedules its next run:

ts
const refreshAgain = () => {
  refreshRequested$.emit(++refreshCount);
  temporal.schedule(refreshAgain, REFRESH_EVERY_MS, {
    owner: 'session-archive',
  });
};
refreshAgain();

After — the stream declares when the query runs and the resource owns its lifetime:

ts
yield *
  query('sessions', {
    method: timer(0, REFRESH_EVERY_MS),
    loader: function* () {
      return yield* loadSessions();
    },
  });

Import timer from @craft-ts/stream. Its first value triggers the initial load, and subsequent values trigger refreshes. The stream is stopped with the resource owner. There is no autofix: ESLint cannot infer whether the first run is immediate or delayed, which value should be emitted as a request parameter, or which resource should own the recurring work. See trigger a resource from a stream.

Scope-matched craft service inputs#

craft-ts/require-craft-service-input-scope is enabled at error in the recommended and Effect presets, including generated apps. It checks that a service factory does not take inputs that its scope cannot own:

  • global factories have no inputs;

  • toProvide and manuallyProvidedAtRoot factories use only $provided;

  • function factories use call-site inputs only; they have no provider for $provided configuration.

Before — a singleton's value depends on whichever consumer supplies it first:

ts
craftService(
  { name: 'UserQuery', providedIn: 'global' },
  function* (inputs: { userId: CraftServiceInput<string> }) {
    // ...
  },
);

Use function when each call has its own inputs. Use a provider scope when consumers should resolve one configured instance; in a component, pass its inputs through withComponentProviders:

ts
craftService(
  { name: 'ProfileContext', providedIn: 'toProvide' },
  function* (inputs: { $provided: { profileId: CraftServiceInput<string> } }) {
    // ...
  },
);

Profile.pipe(
  withComponentProviders(({ profileId }) => [
    provideProfileContext({ profileId }),
  ]),
);

The rule reads inline input types and local type aliases. TypeScript also enforces the scope across aliases and service call sites, where the type system knows which generated helper is being called. See service inputs.

There is no autofix: choose whether the service owns shared component/route state (toProvide) or should create a fresh context for each reusable call (function). Pass provider configuration through $provided, or pass function inputs directly to X(...).

Fixed component provider lists#

craft-ts/require-fixed-component-provider-list is enabled at error in the recommended preset, inherited by the Effect preset and newly generated apps. It requires withComponentProviders to receive a concise arrow returning a literal array with fixed entries and order.

Before — rejected because the component's provider set can change:

ts
Profile.pipe(
  withComponentProviders(({ profileId }) =>
    enabled ? [provideProfileContext({ profileId })] : [],
  ),
);

After — keep the provider present and let its service consume reactive values:

ts
Profile.pipe(
  withComponentProviders(({ profileId }) => [
    provideProfileContext({ profileId, enabled }),
  ]),
);

Here enabled is a reactive reader accepted by the service's configuration. Variables holding lists, block-bodied callbacks, spreads, conditional or logical provider selection, and dynamically assembled lists (map, filter, concat) are rejected. Reactive expressions inside provider arguments are allowed. Renamed imports and namespace imports from @craft-ts/component are recognized; unrelated local functions with the same name are ignored.

There is no autofix: the developer must choose which providers always remain present. This is a local syntax guarantee for the declared list, not an analysis of the implementation of each provider helper. See providers configured by component inputs for the service and component example.

Component inputs with reserved names#

craft-ts/no-reserved-component-input-name is enabled at error in the recommended preset, inherited by the Effect preset and newly generated apps. A component call sends some keys to its root element instead of the component: global DOM properties (id, title, slot, hidden, lang, dir, class, style, …), every data-* and aria-* attribute, and DOM events (error, input, change, load, submit, focus, …) along with their onXxx form. An input declared with one of these names type-checks, but its value becomes an attribute or an event listener of the root element and never reaches the component — a provider configured from it by withComponentProviders receives nothing either.

Before — rejected because title and error never reach Field:

ts
export const Field = craftComponent(
  'Field',
  {},
  (inputs: { title: Input<string>; error: Input<string> }) =>
    span([inputs.title, inputs.error]),
);

After — give each input a component-specific name:

ts
export const Field = craftComponent(
  'Field',
  {},
  (inputs: { titleText: Input<string>; errorMessage: Input<string> }) =>
    span([inputs.titleText, inputs.errorMessage]),
);

// `title` remains available at the call site: it sets the root element's
// DOM attribute, as on any component.
Field({ titleText: 'Email', errorMessage: 'Required', title: 'Your email' });

The rule checks the inputs a craftComponent(...) factory declares (inline types, destructured parameters, local type aliases and interfaces, and imported types under typed linting), never the keys passed at a call site. The reserved vocabulary is the one the @craft-ts/component runtime uses to split a call's keys between the root element and the inputs. There is no autofix: the diagnostic suggests a name prefixed with the component's name (fieldTitle), but renaming an input also changes its callers, so choose the name yourself.

Style modules imported with NodeNext#

craft-ts/style-file-boundary is enabled at error in the recommended preset, inherited by the Effect preset and newly generated apps. A *.style.ts may import another style module, so a design system can be split across several files. Under "moduleResolution": "NodeNext" a relative import has to name the JavaScript output — ./tokens.style.js — and the rule accepts that spelling when the import reaches a typed style module: a tokens.style.ts source (or .tsx) or a tokens.style.d.ts declaration. .mjs maps to .mts/.d.mts and .cjs to .cts/.d.cts, as in TypeScript.

The .js suffix alone proves nothing. If the import lands on a plain tokens.style.js, the values the sheet imports lose their CraftTS token types: TypeScript types them any, or infers whatever the JavaScript happens to produce, so a sheet can spend a value the design system never declared. With typed linting (projectService or project) the rule asks TypeScript which file the import resolved to; without type information it looks for the typed file TypeScript would substitute beside the importing sheet.

Before — rejected because ./tokens.style.js reaches only a plain JavaScript file (or nothing):

ts
// src/tokens.style.js — no tokens.style.ts, no tokens.style.d.ts
export const gap = unit.rem(1);

// src/card.style.ts
import { craftStyles, gap as gapProp } from '@craft-ts/style';
import { gap } from './tokens.style.js'; // ✗ untyped style module

export const card = craftStyles('card', { root: [gapProp(gap)] });

After — the import resolves to the typed source (a tokens.style.d.ts beside a shipped tokens.style.js works the same way):

ts
// src/tokens.style.ts
import { unit } from '@craft-ts/style';

export const gap = unit.rem(1);

// src/card.style.ts
import { craftStyles, gap as gapProp } from '@craft-ts/style';
import { gap } from './tokens.style.js'; // ✓ TypeScript reads tokens.style.ts

export const card = craftStyles('card', { root: [gapProp(gap)] });

./tokens.style and ./tokens.style.ts stay accepted as before. There is no autofix: write the *.style.ts source, or ship its declaration, yourself.

Classes from another package's /style entry#

craft-ts/no-raw-class is enabled at error in the recommended preset, inherited by the Effect preset and newly generated apps. It accepts a class from a project *.style module or from the /style entry of a CraftTS package (@craft-ts/ui/style). A class taken from the /style entry of any other package — @acme/kit/style — stays refused, even when craftStyle({ include: ['@acme/kit'] }) evaluates that package's sheets and the class has CSS.

Loading the package's CSS does not make its classes part of the project's CraftTS token and axis model. Bound directly, the class produces a look nobody can trace back to the project's tokens and axes: its variants are not points of your axes, its colours are not your theme's, and the next component that needs the same styling cannot reuse it consistently. The diagnostic (externalStyleClass) names the import and asks for a local CraftTS adapter: a *.style.ts module in your project that re-expresses what you need with craftStyles, your tokens (cssVars, the palette and scales) and your axes (defineStateAxis, when).

Before — rejected because kit.button comes from an external /style entry:

ts
// src/save.ts
import { button, craftComponent } from '@craft-ts/component';
import { kit } from '@acme/kit/style';

export const Save = craftComponent('Save', {}, () =>
  button(
    'save',
    { type: 'button', class: [kit.button, kit.danger] }, // ✗ externalStyleClass
    'Save',
  ),
);

After — the project's tokens and axes, which the adapter spends:

ts
import { cssVars, defineStateAxis, kind, palette } from '@craft-ts/style';

// The project's own tokens and axes — see "Defining your design system".
const themed = { inherits: true } as const;

export const theme = cssVars('adapterTheme', {
  accent: kind.color(palette.accent.info, themed),
  danger: kind.color(palette.accent.danger, themed),
  onAccent: kind.color(palette.text.inverted, themed),
});

/** Drives `data-tone` on the element that carries it. */
export const tone = defineStateAxis('tone', ['neutral', 'danger']);

The adapter, kit.style.ts, keeps only what the screen needs from the kit, and turns the kit's danger modifier class into a point of the project's tone axis:

ts
import {
  bg,
  color,
  craftStyles,
  fontWeight,
  p,
  radii,
  radius,
  space,
  when,
} from '@craft-ts/style';
import { theme, tone } from './foundation.style';

/**
 * The local CraftTS adapter: what this project needs from the kit's button,
 * re-expressed with the project's own tokens and axes.
 */
export const kitButton = craftStyles(
  'kitButton',
  {
    root: [
      p(space(2)),
      radius(radii.md),
      bg(theme.accent),
      color(theme.onAccent),
      fontWeight.bold,
      // The kit's "danger" modifier becomes a point on the project's axis.
      when(tone.danger, [bg(theme.danger)]),
    ],
  },
  { axes: [tone] },
);

The component binds the adapter's class and sets the axis by attribute:

ts
import { button, craftComponent } from '@craft-ts/component';
// ✓ the project's adapter, not '@acme/kit/style'
import { kitButton } from './kit.style';

export const Save = craftComponent('Save', {}, () =>
  button(
    'save',
    { type: 'button', class: kitButton.root, 'data-tone': 'danger' },
    'Save',
  ),
);

There is no autofix: only you can decide which part of the package's styling the project needs and which of its tokens and axes it maps to. Once nothing binds the package's classes any more, its include entry in craftStyle can go too.

Presets and configuration#

The recommended preset bans every TypeScript assertion in authored Craft code, including as const:

ts
import craftRules from '@craft-ts/dev-tools/eslint-rules';

export default [{ files: ['**/*.ts'], ...craftRules.configs.recommended }];

For a project using @craft-ts/effect, the published preset enables the Craft rules and the Effect adapter rule in one entry:

ts
import craftRules from '@craft-ts/dev-tools/eslint-rules';

export default [
  {
    files: ['**/*.ts'],
    ...craftRules.configs.effect,
  },
];

Use craftRules.configs.recommended for projects that do not use Effect.

Add it to your ESLint flat config:

ts
import craftRules from '@craft-ts/dev-tools/eslint-rules';

export default [
  // keep your existing ESLint config entries
  {
    files: ['**/*.ts'],
    plugins: {
      'craft-ts': craftRules,
    },
    rules: {
      'craft-ts/prefer-craft-template-blocks': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-render-writes': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-reactive-template-bindings': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-craft-use': 'warn',
      'craft-ts/no-craft-service-return': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-mutable-craft-service-closure-state': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-craft-service-input-scope': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-craft-component-return-type': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-reserved-component-input-name': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-craft-component-for-exported-node-factory': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-raw-craft-router-url': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-type-assertions-in-template': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-explicit-craft-template-return-type': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-extracted-craft-component-parts': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-direct-craft-component-template': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-ephemeral-template-form-state': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-form-for-input-action': 'error',
      'craft-ts/template-element-name-unique': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-craft-computed-side-effects': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-external-state-transition': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-craft-method-for-yieldable-callback': 'error',
      'craft-ts/prefer-direct-yieldable-callback': 'error',
      'craft-ts/prefer-deep-yieldable-for-item': 'warn',
      'craft-ts/require-yieldable-reactive-read': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-yieldable-template-method': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-yieldable-insertion-write': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-craft-service-component-same-file': 'error',
      'craft-ts/max-craft-declarations-per-file': 'error',
      'craft-ts/max-craft-component-lines': 'warn',
      'craft-ts/prefer-craft-http-transport': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-injection-token': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-primitive-derived-property': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-reused-primitive-method': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-async-await': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-throw': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-recursive-craft-schedule': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-imperative-craft-resource-trigger': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-imperative-craft-method-actions': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-remote-work-in-craft-method': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-type-assertions-in-resource-loader': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-explicit-resource-loader-type': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-explicit-craft-insertion-type': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-craft-primitive-type-assertion': 'error',
      'craft-ts/prefer-insert-deep-yieldable': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-imperative-template-action-chain': 'error',
      'craft-ts/prefer-route-query-params-for-filter-state': 'warn',
      'craft-ts/no-imperative-storage-in-craft-method': 'error',
      'craft-ts/no-transition-actions': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-craft-resource-trigger-yield': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-assert-exhaustive-route-exceptions': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-craft-exception-handler': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-catch-tag-exhaustive-reaction': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-exception-component-di-check': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-pending-component-di-check': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-child-route-mount-check': 'error',
      'craft-ts/require-lazy-load-with-retry': 'error',
      'craft-ts/global-exception-registry-match': 'error',
    },
  },
];

What each rule does:

  • craft-ts/prefer-craft-template-blocks: keeps craftComponent(...) templates declarative by rejecting ternaries, boolean logical expressions, negations, and imperative control flow; nullish value fallbacks remain valid. Use ifNode(...), matchNode.exhaustive(...), forNode(...), or deferNode(...) for render control flow

  • craft-ts/require-craft-computed-for-dynamic-template-lookup: rejects dynamic object or array lookups in a Craft template when the lookup key comes from a reactive member; move the lookup to a named craftComputed() in the component's service and bind that value directly

  • craft-ts/no-render-writes: rejects detectable set(), update(), and mutate() calls in component templates and render bindings while allowing DOM event and onXxx output callbacks

  • craft-ts/no-external-state-transition: rejects generic replace, set, update, or patch calls on a value returned by Craft state(...) outside its state insertion. Put the transition behind a named state method that accepts intent and computes the next value internally.

  • craft-ts/no-imported-state-actions: rejects mutable actions on imported bindings, including inside Craft callbacks. Resolve the owner through Craft DI and pass the needed capability as an explicit function input; the rule has no autofix.

  • craft-ts/no-state-facade: rejects custom callable state types that combine a synchronous mutation method with a reader. Expose state operations through a state(...) insertion and delegate writes with yield*.

  • craft-ts/require-reactive-template-bindings: requires signals, named Craft values, and component inputs to be read inside granular binding callbacks instead of during VNode construction; also keeps derived helper calls and data transformations out of those bindings. Static values, Craft readers, presentation conversions, message-catalog interpolation, renderer calls, and event/output callbacks remain valid.

  • craft-ts/no-craft-use: warns when craftUse(...) appears outside a test file. In business code, prefer a named Craft primitive and yield* in its generator. Keep craftUse for synchronous test boundaries, including focused tests of a generator.

  • craft-ts/no-craft-service-return: forbids returning a value from a craftService factory. Its API is assembled from the named values yielded by its generator; use yield* craftPrivate(...) for primitives that should stay internal, and craftExpose(name, value) for standalone values that belong in the API. The rule autofixes simple returned objects whose properties already match yielded primitive names.

  • craft-ts/no-mutable-craft-service-closure-state: rejects writes to service-local variables from direct craftExpose(...) callbacks, including assignments, increments, and property assignments. Declare persistent values with state(...) and expose transitions through its insertion; helper-delegated writes are outside this rule's static analysis.

  • craft-ts/no-duplicate-craft-service-exposure: requires each public key in a craftService to occur once, including keys created by named utilities such as state(...) and keys created by craftExpose(...). Remove a duplicate exposure or choose a distinct key for a standalone value; the rule does not autofix because removing an API key can affect consumers.

  • craft-ts/no-reexposed-craft-service-utility: forbids passing a locally declared, publicly yielded utility result back to craftExpose(...) under a different key. The utility is already available by its declared key; remove the redundant call and keep the existing key. The rule does not autofix.

  • craft-ts/require-craft-service-input-scope: keeps global services input-free, limits provider-scoped services to $provided, and checks function-scoped inputs. TypeScript also rejects invalid service-helper bindings at call sites.

  • craft-ts/prefer-direct-craft-service-exposure: reports craftExpose(...) wrappers that repeat a yielded service's name, a named primitive result, or a member already returned by a primitive such as state, including when the member is renamed; keep the existing nested path (for example, View.searchInput.setSearchInput). It also reports a member destructured from a yielded service only to be exposed again: expose it from the shortcut with craftExpose('save', View.save), or yield View.count() when the member is a reader (calling a shortcut runs a method). It forbids craftExpose inside supported primitive declarations or callbacks. Keep craftExpose for standalone or computed values.

  • craft-ts/prefer-craft-computed-for-reactive-generator: reports a zero-argument generator exposed as a service value when its only statement returns a value derived from a yield* read. Declare that value with yield* craftComputed(name, function* () { ... }); parameterized generators and multi-step workflows are unaffected.

  • craft-ts/prefer-craft-computed-for-reactive-array-length: reports .length reads from reactive array readers in consumers. Expose a boolean or count through craftComputed in the owning service; .length inside that computed is allowed, and no autofix is offered because the scalar API needs a domain-specific name.

  • craft-ts/prefer-computed-local-dependency: reports a dependency yielded outside a craftComputed when every use of that dependency is inside that computed and craft-ts/no-craft-computed-side-effects would accept it there (a reactive read, CraftRouter(), CraftGlobalError(), a proven i18n reader — see Only provable reads go inside a craftComputed). Yield it in a generator callback there so the computed records its own dependency; no autofix is offered because the callback may need to become a generator. A service whose resolution is not proven pure stays resolved by the enclosing body.

  • craft-ts/require-craft-component-for-exported-node-factory: requires an exported function that directly returns a Craft node, such as button(...), to be declared with craftComponent(...) so Craft directives and composition remain available

Keep craftService exposure keys unique#

Named utilities yielded directly from a craftService are already exposed under their declared name. craftExpose also adds a public key, so the same key must not be used by another utility or another craftExpose call.

This rule catches key collisions, even when the values are different. The next rule catches the other case: exposing the same yielded utility again under a different key. Both checks protect the service API, but they diagnose different mistakes.

Before — expanded is exposed by state(...) and then exposed again:

ts
const expanded = yield * state('expanded', false);

// ❌ `expanded` is already a public service key
yield * craftExpose('expanded', expanded);

After — yield the primitive once; the service exposes it under expanded:

ts
yield * state('expanded', false);

The rule also catches duplicate standalone keys:

ts
// ❌ both values claim the same public key
yield * craftExpose('format', formatDate);
yield * craftExpose('format', formatCurrency);

// ✅ each value has its own key
yield * craftExpose('formatDate', formatDate);
yield * craftExpose('formatCurrency', formatCurrency);

Do not re-expose a declared service utility#

no-duplicate-craft-service-exposure catches repeated keys. This rule catches re-exporting the same utility under a different key: a public utility yielded from state, query, mutation, or another named primitive already has an API path, so adding an alias with craftExpose creates a redundant second path.

Before — the local variable is the already-public state('language') utility:

ts
const language = yield * state('language', 'en');

// ❌ creates a second path to the same utility
yield * craftExpose('locale', language);

After — keep the primitive's public language key:

ts
yield * state('language', 'en');

Neither rule offers eslint --fix: removing or renaming a key can change the service API, so the author must choose the intended public name and update its consumers.

Avoid flattening primitive members with craftExpose#

Members returned from a named primitive are already available below that primitive in the service API. Re-exporting one with craftExpose creates a second, flat access path and can make the two paths drift apart.

Before — the method is already available through searchInput:

ts
const searchInput =
  yield *
  state('searchInput', '', ({ set }) => ({
    setSearchInput: (value: string) => set(value),
  }));

// ❌ duplicates searchInput.setSearchInput on the service API
yield * craftExpose('setSearchInput', searchInput.setSearchInput);

After — keep the member under its primitive and update consumers to use that path:

ts
const searchInput =
  yield *
  state('searchInput', '', ({ set }) => ({
    setSearchInput: (value: string) => set(value),
  }));

yield * View.searchInput.setSearchInput(value);

The rule catches these members even when the first craftExpose argument renames them. It also catches methods and properties returned by query, mutation, asyncProcess, and queryParams. It only reports when the matching member is visible in the primitive's returned object and the primitive is publicly yielded. eslint --fix does not rewrite this: update consumers to the nested path, then remove the redundant craftExpose call.

Small node factories are valid when they stay private to the file:

ts
function filterButton(filter: TodoFilter, label: string) {
  return button('todoFilterButton', { type: 'button' }, label);
}

Once the function is exported, use a Craft component so directives and composition can be applied at the module boundary:

ts
// ❌ craft-ts/require-craft-component-for-exported-node-factory
export function filterButton(filter: TodoFilter, label: string) {
  return button('todoFilterButton', { type: 'button' }, label);
}

// ✅
export const FilterButton = craftComponent(
  'FilterButton',
  {},
  ({
    label,
  }: {
    readonly filter: Input<TodoFilter>;
    readonly label: Input<string>;
  }) => button('todoFilterButton', { type: 'button' }, label),
);

The rule also follows named exports such as export { filterButton } and checks exported arrow functions.

  • craft-ts/no-type-assertions-in-template: forbids as ... and angle-bracket type assertions in Craft templates; fix the type in the component's service or expose a correctly typed derived value

  • craft-ts/no-explicit-craft-template-return-type: forbids explicit return annotations on render callbacks inside craftComponent(...). A broad annotation such as (): CraftNodeChildren widens the concrete node type, breaks dependency and type-safe DI inference, and can surface as a runtime error. Let the callback return type be inferred:

    ts
    const pendingStatusMessage = (message: string) => p(message);

// ❌ The annotation erases the concrete node/dependency information.
pendingNode({
  fallback: (): CraftNodeChildren => pendingStatusMessage('Loading…'),
  reloading: (): CraftNodeChildren => pendingStatusMessage('Reloading…'),
});

// ✅ The concrete `p(...)` node stays visible to Craft's inference.
pendingNode({
  fallback: () => pendingStatusMessage('Loading…'),
  reloading: () => pendingStatusMessage('Reloading…'),
});

    The rule is autofixable with eslint --fix. Return annotations on DOM event and output callbacks remain allowed because those callbacks do not produce rendered children.

  • craft-ts/no-extracted-craft-component-parts: requires the function passed to craftComponent(...) to stay inline. Keeping it at the component boundary preserves contextual type inference and makes the component's behaviour readable in one place.

    Before — an extracted ReviewTemplate hides the component's two halves behind names at the call site:

    ts
    // ❌ craft-ts/no-extracted-craft-component-parts
const ReviewTemplate = craftTemplate(({ decide }) =>
  div([button({ click: decide }, 'Review')]),
);

export const ReviewApp = craftComponent('ReviewApp', {}, ReviewTemplate);

    After — keep a concise template lambda in the component call:

    ts
    // ✅
export const ReviewApp = craftComponent('ReviewApp', {}, () =>
  div([button('review', { type: 'button' }, 'Review')]),
);

    The rule only rejects an identifier in the template argument position. The direct concise arrow is the supported form for a component template; use the returned node expression inline so craftComponent(...) can contextually type it.

  • craft-ts/require-direct-craft-component-template: requires the third argument to craftComponent(...) to be a concise arrow function whose body directly constructs a template node or node array. Keep service setup, destructuring, aliases, and other statements outside the component template; expose the values the template needs through its view API. The lambda's parameters may be named inputs, but may not destructure them. Render and event callbacks inside the returned tree are unaffected.

    Before — the component factory resolves a service, destructures its result, and only then builds the template:

    ts
    // ❌ craft-ts/require-direct-craft-component-template
const PixelArt = craftComponent(
  'PixelArt',
  { providers: [providePixelArtView()] },
  function* () {
    const { cells, renderedPixelGrid } = yield* PixelArtView();
    return section({ class: example.card }, [
      button('clear', { click: cells.clearAll }, 'Clear'),
      div({ class: pixel.grid, role: 'grid' }, renderedPixelGrid),
    ]);
  },
);

    After — return the section(...) directly and read each value where it is used. This form assumes PixelArtView exposes those members on its view API:

    ts
    // ✅
const PixelArt = craftComponent(
  'PixelArt',
  { providers: [providePixelArtView()] },
  () =>
    section({ class: example.card }, [
      button('clear', { click: PixelArtView.cells.clearAll }, 'Clear'),
      div(
        { class: pixel.grid, role: 'grid' },
        PixelArtView.renderedPixelGrid,
      ),
    ]),
);

  • craft-ts/no-ephemeral-template-form-state: forbids let / const / var in a craftComponent(...) or craftDirective(...) template. Component templates now return their node tree directly, so state and derived values belong in a view service; directive generator templates must also avoid render-local state because they can rerun.

  • craft-ts/require-form-for-input-action: rejects a button's direct mutate(...) or method(...) call when it consumes an input-bound value, including through a local record or variable; use insertForm, insertFormAttributes, and insertFormSubmit for mutation-backed forms, then submit a native form(...) with a type: 'submit' button

  • craft-ts/template-element-name-unique: requires named HTML helpers to use a static, unique local name within a component; use the object-first helper form for unnamed elements such as p({ id: 'hint' }, ...)

  • craft-ts/no-craft-computed-side-effects: forbids writes, asynchronous work and unproven service resolution inside craftComputed; only reactive reads, settled(...), syncEffect(...), the synchronous core capabilities and proven i18n readers are allowed (see Only provable reads go inside a craftComputed). The graph-wide counterpart is assertCraftComputedPure.

  • craft-ts/no-effect-outside-loaders: keeps params, methods, craftComputed(...), and craftEffect(...) synchronous by allowing Effect values and Effect service reads only in Effect loaders; no-effect-in-params remains as a compatibility alias

  • craft-ts/sync-effect-body: keeps a body declared synchronous (SyncOp in its requirements) free of anything that may suspend — async constructors such as Effect.sleep/Effect.promise, and members nothing declares synchronous. Type-aware: the ESLint parser must use projectService: true or a TypeScript project

  • craft-ts/no-explicit-effect-type: lets Effect.gen infer its complete type instead of repeating an explicit Effect annotation; contracts declared in interfaces and type aliases remain allowed

  • craft-ts/prefer-inline-effect-insertion: keeps the queryEffect insertion factory inline so its resource and exception types are inferred without a separate InsertionParams context alias

  • craft-ts/prefer-inline-route-providers: inlines a route provider tuple used only once by loadCraftComponent(...), preserving the route-level type proof

  • craft-ts/prefer-craft-reactivity: rejects authored signal/computed/effect/resource APIs, explicit .subscribe() calls, and RxJS Subject/BehaviorSubject/ReplaySubject; use state, craftComputed, craftEffect, query, and named source$/on$ flows

  • craft-ts/prefer-craft-service: keeps services in the craftService(...) model

  • craft-ts/no-craft-service-component-same-file: forbids declaring craftService(...) and craftComponent(...) in the same file; a route-level service provider combined with a lazy-loaded component can break lazy loading, so keep them in separate files

  • craft-ts/max-craft-declarations-per-file: reports the third and subsequent craftComponent(...), craftService(...), or craftDirective(...) declaration of the same kind in a file; keep Craft entities split across focused files

  • craft-ts/max-craft-component-lines: reports a file that declares a craftComponent(...) once it exceeds 700 non-import lines (import statements and blank lines are not counted, so a component with many dependencies is not penalized for its import block). A file this long usually mixes business logic, view logic, and markup that could live in separate, independently testable units:

    ts
    // ❌ craft-ts/max-craft-component-lines
// review-app.ts — 3894 lines: filtering, sorting, diff computation,
// pagination, and the full markup tree inlined in one component.
export const ReviewApp = craftComponent(
  'ReviewApp',
  {},
  function* (inputs: { readonly subjects: Input<Subject[]> }) {
    const filtered = yield* craftComputed(
      'filtered',
      () => /* 80 lines */ [],
    );
    const diff = yield* craftComputed(
      'diff',
      () => /* 150 lines of diffing */ null,
    );
    // …dozens more computeds and craftMethods…

    return div(
      {},
      /* a thousand-plus lines of markup for the filter bar, the diff
         viewport, the review card list, and the pagination controls */
    );
  },
);

// ✅ Business logic moves to a craftService; independent template
// regions become their own craftComponent, each testable and readable
// on its own.
export const { ReviewFilters } = craftService(
  { name: 'ReviewFilters', providedIn: 'global' },
  function* () {
    yield* craftExpose(
      'filter',
      (subjects: Subject[], criteria: FilterCriteria) => /* … */ [],
    );
  },
);

export const SubjectDiffViewport = craftComponent(
  'SubjectDiffViewport',
  {},
  ({ subject }: { readonly subject: Input<Subject> }) => div({} /* … */),
);

export const ReviewApp = craftComponent(
  'ReviewApp',
  { providers: [provideReviewAppView()] },
  function* (inputs: { readonly subjects: Input<Subject[]> }) {
    const { filtered } = yield* ReviewAppView(inputs);

    return div(
      {},
      forNode(filtered, (subject) => SubjectDiffViewport({ subject })),
    );
  },
);

    Set a project-specific threshold with ['warn', { max: 600 }] if 700 lines is still too generous for your team.

  • craft-ts/no-injection-token: forbids authored InjectionToken contracts; declare them with craftService({ name, providedIn: 'abstract' }, abstract<Contract>())

  • craft-ts/prefer-craft-http-client: forbids direct transport usage in favor of CraftHttpClient

  • craft-ts/prefer-craft-http-transport: forbids direct fetch() and XMLHttpRequest because they bypass typed responses and exceptions, tracing, cancellation, and the architecture graph; use query() for reads or mutation() for writes with CraftHttpClient, or CraftBinaryHttpClient for raw binary bodies

require-server-function-codec#

Client-exposed server functions declare a schema on both sides of the transport: the input schema decodes and validates the incoming value, and the output schema validates the result before it is encoded for the client. These contracts also let scenario catalogs encode deterministic recipe mocks.

Before — a boundary whose input or result shape is implicit:

typescript
serverFunction('orders.list', inputSchema, { exposure: 'client' });

After — both transport directions have a declared schema:

typescript
serverFunction('orders.list', inputSchema, {
  exposure: 'client',
  output: ordersSchema,
});

The rule reports the missing input decoder or output encoder separately. There is no automatic fix because choosing the correct schema is a domain decision. An opaque third-party protocol may set codecExemption to a specific reason and handling location; vague or empty exemptions fail lint.

  • craft-ts/prefer-craft-input-output: keeps component inputs and outputs in the Input/Output model used by craftComponent(...)

  • craft-ts/require-primitive-derived-property: requires a computed or craftComputed that only depends on one primitive in the same component/service to be exposed by that primitive's insertion, including directly yielded named craftComputed values; simple cases are autofixed

  • craft-ts/no-reused-primitive-method: requires an exposed primitive insertion method to have one call site per file, including unchanged aliases; naming an alias is not a call site, binding it is. Create a context-specific insertion method for each distinct use

  • craft-ts/prefer-craft-long-press: reports a local pointer/touch hold implementation that combines a start event, release/cancel events, and a timer. Use longPress from @craft-ts/core; for a genuinely custom gesture, declare its semantic replay boundary with runCraftReplayTrigger(...). No autofix is offered because replacing a gesture requires choosing its handler and options.

  • craft-ts/prefer-craft-pointer-gestures: reports native pointer listeners with coordinate tracking and drag/swipe phases. Use drag or swipe from @craft-ts/core; keep high-frequency preview work presentation-only and put semantic work in the terminal callback. No autofix is offered because gesture intent and thresholds need a human choice.

  • craft-ts/require-craft-replay-trigger: reports a direct native gesture listener whose callback contains a Craft generator or executeYieldable(...) without runCraftReplayTrigger(...). Visual-only listeners and Craft template event bindings remain valid; the rule only claims the callback shapes it can recognize in the current file.

  • craft-ts/no-async-await: forbids async functions, await, and for await...of because native Promise suspension hides Craft dependencies and can lose cancellation or exception tracking; use generator-based Craft primitives, craftSleep, and CraftHttpClient instead

  • craft-ts/require-loop-sleep-or-stop: requires a while / do / for driven by yield* or true to suspend on craftSleep (cancelled with its owner) or to have a break, return or throw; without either it re-runs as fast as the runtime allows. See page stability

  • craft-ts/no-recursive-craft-schedule: reports a function passed to schedule(...) from inside that same function, including direct variable aliases. Use timer(...) from @craft-ts/stream as the resource method to declare recurring query, mutation, or async process triggers. The rule does not autofix because it cannot infer cadence, initial trigger timing, or emitted request parameters; see the stream migration example.

  • craft-ts/require-generator-resource-loader: requires query, mutation, and asyncProcess loaders to be generator functions because a plain or async return hides remote dependencies from the resource lifecycle; use yield* to keep each suspension tracked

  • craft-ts/no-throw: forbids throw in Craft code because it bypasses the typed resource exception channel, and offers a Quick Fix that returns craftException({ _tag: 'UNEXPECTED_ERROR' }, { error: ... }); keep technical boundaries and tests outside this rule when their contracts require thrown errors

  • craft-ts/no-imperative-craft-resource-trigger: forbids query.call(...), mutation.mutate(...), and asyncProcess.method(...) in a craftEffect dependency graph, including through craftGen(...). The graph-wide counterpart, including state / source$ writes, is assertCraftEffectNoImperativeSync.

  • craft-ts/no-imperative-craft-method-actions: forbids composing multiple imperative actions in a craftMethod; emit a source$ event and let the affected query react with insertReactOnMutation(...) instead. It also reports repeated state.set / state.update calls on the same state across methods exposed with craftExpose(...), and writes to multiple states in one block of an exposed craftService method; emit one source event and let each state react with on$(...). A handler such as event.preventDefault() followed by one mutation.mutate(...) remains valid. The rule checks exposed named functions and direct state writes, so it does not claim to detect every possible control-flow path.

When one replay operation changes several pieces of state, keep the imperative method to one event emission. The state owner describes the resulting updates:

typescript
// Before: the exposed method coordinates state updates itself.
function clearImportedSession() {
  session.set(undefined);
  events.set([]);
  loadError.set(undefined);
}

// After: one event carries the intent; each state reacts to it.
const clearImportedSession$ = source$<void>('clearImportedSession');

const session = state('session', initialSession, ({ set }) => ({
  clearOnImport: on$(clearImportedSession$, () => set(undefined)),
}));
const events = state('events', initialEvents, ({ set }) => ({
  clearOnImport: on$(clearImportedSession$, () => set([])),
}));
const loadError = state('loadError', undefined, ({ set }) => ({
  clearOnImport: on$(clearImportedSession$, () => set(undefined)),
}));

function clearImportedSession() {
  clearImportedSession$.emit();
}

craft-ts/no-reused-primitive-method rejects reusing one exposed primitive insertion method at multiple call sites in a file. The graph-wide assertPrimitiveMethodsUsedOnce check enforces that invariant across the application. The craftExpose(...) check above applies the same single-callsite constraint to direct set / update calls on a state binding. When several states must respond to one operation, use a shared source$ and on$(...).

  • craft-ts/no-event-only-craft-method: errors by default when a craftMethod only calls preventDefault(), stopPropagation(), or stopImmediatePropagation() and then delegates to one action. Bind the action with eventAction(...) on the element. The default architecture check enforces the same rule across files.

  • craft-ts/no-remote-work-in-craft-method: forbids CraftHttpClient.*(...) inside craftMethod because that action boundary does not own request loading, cancellation, exceptions, or graph dependencies; define the request directly in the query or mutation loader.

  • craft-ts/no-type-assertions-in-resource-loader: forbids as ... and angle-bracket assertions inside query, mutation, and asyncProcess loaders because assertions only silence TypeScript and can hide Promise, response, or transport mismatches; repair the request or adapter typing instead.

  • craft-ts/no-type-assertions-in-craft-code: forbids TypeScript type assertions in authored Craft code, including as const and angle-bracket assertions; the narrow undefined as T | undefined seed is allowed for intentionally optional state values. Use correct API typing or satisfies for shape validation. Low-level technical adapters may disable this rule locally when an explicit runtime boundary cast is unavoidable.

  • craft-ts/no-explicit-resource-loader-type: forbids explicit parameter and return annotations on query, mutation, and asyncProcess loaders; let the resource infer its contract from params, method, and the yielded operations instead of writing Generator<...> or { params: string }

  • craft-ts/no-explicit-craft-insertion-type: forbids explicit parameter and return annotations on callbacks passed to insert*Pipe; let the primitive infer the insertion context and derived output

  • craft-ts/no-craft-primitive-type-assertion: forbids chained assertions such as as unknown as Generator<...> around Craft primitive generators, which can hide the inferred output and dependency contract

  • craft-ts/prefer-insert-deep-yieldable: rejects adapting a property of a primitive result with deepYieldable(...); add insertDeepYieldable() to the primitive and read the property directly

  • craft-ts/no-imperative-template-action-chain: forbids chaining multiple Craft actions in one template event callback, or in a generator passed as a component prop (trigger: function* () { … }); it also follows named event handlers from the legacy four-argument craftComponent(...) form. Emit one source$ event and let the query, mutation, and state react through on$. With type information, any yield* of a service method counts as an action (yield* View.label.recordConfirm()), whatever its name; yield* of a reactive reader does not (const user = yield* View.user()), so a handler can read as many values as it needs around a single action

  • craft-ts/prefer-route-query-params-for-filter-state: warns when a local state() is used directly or through a local derivation as params for query, queryEffect, asyncProcess, or asyncProcessEffect; use queryParams() for values that should survive reloads and be represented in the URL. The graph-wide counterpart, which also sees cross-file dependencies, is assertResourceParamsPreferQueryParams.

  • craft-ts/no-imperative-storage-in-craft-method: forbids direct storage access and imperative location changes in a craftMethod; use insertReactOnMutation(...) with optimisticUpdate: () => undefined to clear the affected query and let its persistence follow the query state.

  • craft-ts/no-transition-actions: forbids query.call(...), mutation.mutate(...), asyncProcess.method(...), state.restore(...), and source$.emit(...) inside transitionStep(...). Trace the event's producer first: emit external events at their real boundary and consume them with on$(source$, ...); for values derived by afterRecomputation(...), keep the value in the machine, register the reaction under its destination transitionStep(...), and pass it to transit(value) with a transitionGuard(({ from, event }) => ...). transit() targets the step that declares it. If this requires an insertion-level currentStep() router or state changes after acceptance, treat it as an API gap. See Recomputations as transition triggers.

  • craft-ts/require-craft-resource-trigger-yield: requires those triggers to use yield* inside generator functions, while ordinary UI callbacks may keep imperative calls

  • craft-ts/require-craft-method-for-yieldable-callback: requires an event callback in a craftComponent template — a DOM event prop (click, change, onClick, …) or a component Output — to wrap yieldable Craft method calls in craftMethod(...); render callbacks such as matchNode handlers, forNode renders or slots are not checked. See Wrap event callbacks that call yieldable methods

  • craft-ts/prefer-direct-yieldable-callback: replaces a template generator or generator method that only delegates yield* callback() with the callback reference itself (callback or object.method)

  • craft-ts/prefer-direct-yieldable-destructuring: inlines a yield* result into its only object destructuring

  • craft-ts/prefer-deep-yieldable-for-item: warns when a forNode item is read repeatedly through yield* item() property accesses; expose a named insertDeepYieldable('property') collection and use direct item property readers

  • craft-ts/require-yieldable-reactive-read: requires Craft reactive readers to be delegated with yield* inside generator functions; a named ifNode condition callback may return one reader invocation directly

  • craft-ts/no-craft-computed-in-component: forbids craftComputed(...) in a craftComponent(...) factory; expose the derived reader from a craftService(...) and keep the component focused on rendering.

  • craft-ts/no-component-service-binding: forbids binding a yielded service result in the component factory; read it in the template callback where it is consumed.

  • craft-ts/require-yieldable-template-method: requires yieldable Craft method calls in a craftComponent template to be delegated with yield*, or passed as a reference (click: counter.increment)

  • craft-ts/require-yieldable-insertion-write: requires set(...), patch(...), and update(...) to be delegated with yield* when they are used inside a generator method

  • craft-ts/require-assert-exhaustive-route-exceptions: adds the collection-level assertExhaustiveRouteExceptions(...) safety net

  • craft-ts/require-craft-exception-handler: enforces craftExceptionHandler(function* (...) {}); simple handlers are autofixed and ambiguous raw redirects are reported for manual migration

  • craft-ts/require-catch-tag-exhaustive-reaction: rejects empty catchTag.exhaustive handlers and bare return; statements so each caught exception triggers a real reaction

  • craft-ts/require-exception-component-di-check: generates O(1) RouteExceptionComponentCheckedDI checks for renderComponent, route-level errorComponent, withErrorComponent, withRouteLoadError, and route-local provideRouteLoadErrorComponent

  • craft-ts/require-pending-component-di-check: generates the independent RouteCheckedDI check for each pendingComponent

  • craft-ts/no-raw-class: requires every class: binding — on an element, in attrs, on a component host — to trace back to a sheet imported from a *.style module: sheet.key, a const bound to one, an array of them, a typed input (a parameter or a member of one), or a function that only returns one. A string, a template literal, a conditional or an object of booleans is refused. A class assembled at render time is a visual state nothing recorded, so the visual matrix would enumerate what the sheets declare while the DOM shows something else; and a sheet declared outside a *.style.ts is never evaluated by the build, so its class has no CSS. Make the variation an axis and set a data-* attribute. A class from the /style entry of a package outside @craft-ts (@acme/kit/style) is refused with its own message: wrap what you need in a local CraftTS adapter

  • craft-ts/no-inline-style: restricts style: to assign(...) from @craft-ts/style — or an array of them, an object spreading only them, a conditional whose branches are all of them, or a function that only returns them. What varies at runtime is a typed variable (cssVars + assign), read by a sheet; attrs.style is always refused

  • craft-ts/no-component-css: forbids every .css import except virtual:craft-style.css. Global rules go in craftGlobalStyles, fonts in defineFont

  • craft-ts/no-forbidden-eslint-disable: requires a reason on every directive that disables a design-system rule — // eslint-disable-next-line craft-ts/no-raw-class -- markdown output carries its own classes. The reason is what the reviewer decides on in Review Attest. It also forbids disabling the rules listed in .craft/eslint-disable-policy.json. A blanket eslint-disable silences this rule too, so it cannot be reported here; Review Attest lists it

  • craft-ts/no-raw-css-value: forbids a string or number literal as an argument to a @craft-ts/style helper — p('12px'), bg('red'). If the scale is missing the step, add it to the scale; if the value genuinely cannot be proven, unsafeLength('13px', reason) compiles and makes the debt countable in the graph. A variable read written as a string — color('var(--host-accent)') — is reported as rawVar: declare the variable with cssVars(...) when the view owns it; when the host page owns it, import the host's CraftTS style contract, or write an adapter that provides one (variables owned by the host page)

  • craft-ts/no-free-has: forbids a hand-written :has() in styles. It reaches across the component boundary, so what a component looks like depends on markup it does not own — a state the matrix cannot enumerate. Use the descendant axis, which is a closed set and carries its own test driver

  • craft-ts/style-file-boundary: restricts a *.style.ts to style-vocabulary imports. The build plugin imports the file in Node to read what it registered, so an application import would run application code at build time. A relative import of another style module may use the NodeNext spelling (./tokens.style.js) only when it reaches a typed *.style.ts source or *.style.d.ts declaration; see Style modules imported with NodeNext

  • craft-ts/require-effect-adapters: requires the Effect-aware adapters — queryEffect, mutationEffect, asyncProcessEffect, and transitionGuardEffect — instead of the plain primitives and transitionGuard in an Effect application. A query whose loader yields an imported CraftHttpClient request stays a Craft query because that request is a Craft generator, not an Effect; server-function queries follow the same boundary. See Choose the right adapter

  • craft-ts/craft-signal-source-name-match: requires signalSource(name, ...) to take a string literal matching the variable, class property or object property it is assigned to, so the name in a trace is the name in the source. A computed name defeats the architecture graph, which reads these names statically

  • craft-ts/require-child-route-mount-check: adds the missing assertChildRouteMounts(...) call + import (Quick Fix) for any craftRoutes(...) collection that mounts lazy loadChildren, so a .withParent-pinned child mounted under the wrong path is a compile error

  • craft-ts/require-lazy-load-with-retry: wraps route loadComponent and loadChildren imports with the generated withRetry(...) loader helper while preserving a statically analyzable import specifier

  • craft-ts/global-exception-registry-match: keeps CraftGlobalExceptionRegistry synchronized with handlers delegating to globalError()

  • craft-ts/prefer-craft-router-link: requires CraftRouterLink for app-relative Craft anchor hrefs, and reports ambiguous dynamic hrefs; external URLs, fragment links, downloads, _blank, and links marked with data-navigation: 'external' remain native. No autofix is offered because the author must choose the declared route and its parameters.

  • craft-ts/no-manual-craft-routing: rejects browser URL parsing and History API/event handling used to match, select, or change Craft routes; use CraftActivatedRoute with typed path/query helpers to read the route, CraftRouter.navigate(...) for actions, and CraftRouterLink(...) for links. No autofix is offered because route ownership and parameter mapping require a human choice.

  • craft-ts/prefer-craft-route-over-page-state: warns when string-valued state named page, currentPage, activePage, or routePage may duplicate route activation; if it chooses the visible app page, declare routes with craftRoutes(...) and render them with CraftRouterOutlet(). Pagination and page-local state remain valid. Warning only; no autofix.

  • craft-ts/no-raw-craft-router-url: rejects reading CraftRouter.url; use the typed route parameter helper generated by craftRoutes(...) instead of parsing the URL

  • craft-ts/no-craft-component-return-type: rejects explicit annotations on craftComponent(...) results so dependency and template inference remains intact

  • craft-ts/no-reserved-component-input-name: rejects craftComponent(...) inputs named like a DOM property (title, id, slot, …), a data-*/aria-* attribute or a DOM event (error, input, onClick, …); a component call sends those keys to its root element, so the input would never reach the component. See component inputs with reserved names

Keep derived state in services#

craft-ts/no-craft-computed-in-component is an error in the recommended and Effect presets, including generated apps. A component consumes its view service and renders its readers; the service owns derived values.

Before — the component derives a filtered list from a data service:

ts
export const ItemList = craftComponent('ItemList', {}, function* () {
  const store = yield* ItemStore();
  const visibleItems = yield* craftComputed('visibleItems', function* () {
    const items = yield* store.items();
    return items.filter((item) => item.visible);
  });
  return ul(forNode(visibleItems, { track: (item) => item.id }, renderItem));
});

After — the service owns the derivation and the component renders it:

ts
export const { ItemListView } = craftService(
  { name: 'itemListView', providedIn: 'global' },
  function* () {
    const store = yield* ItemStore();
    yield* craftComputed('visibleItems', function* () {
      const items = yield* store.items();
      return items.filter((item) => item.visible);
    });
  },
);

export const ItemList = craftComponent('ItemList', {}, function* () {
  const { visibleItems } = yield* ItemListView();
  return ul(forNode(visibleItems, { track: (item) => item.id }, renderItem));
});

There is no autofix: moving a derivation requires choosing its service scope and updating the service's exposed interface.

Read service values where the template uses them#

craft-ts/no-component-service-binding is an error in the recommended and Effect presets. It reports a const bound to a yielded service result, values destructured from that result, and aliases of those values in the craftComponent(...) factory. Read each service value inside the template binding that consumes it.

Before — the component factory keeps a service result for a later callback:

ts
export const ReplayPanel = craftComponent('ReplayPanel', {}, function* () {
  const replay = yield* ReplaySession();
  return button('pause', {
    type: 'button',
    click: function* () {
      replay.seekReplayBeforeSequence(0);
    },
  });
});

After — the event binding resolves the service at its use site:

ts
export const ReplayPanel = craftComponent('ReplayPanel', {}, function* () {
  return button('pause', {
    type: 'button',
    click: function* () {
      (yield* ReplaySession()).seekReplayBeforeSequence(0);
    },
  });
});

The rule allows yielded service reads inside template callbacks and does not autofix, because each value must be moved to the template binding that owns its use.

Promise and transport boundaries#

These rules protect the same boundary: asynchronous work must remain visible to the Craft resource that owns it. A native Promise may eventually resolve, but it does not describe which Craft dependencies were read, where suspension occurred, or which resource should be cancelled and receive the exception.

Keep resource loaders generator-based#

ts
// Incorrect: the native Promise hides the request from the Craft lifecycle.
query('usersQuery', {
  loader: async () => (await fetch('/api/users')).json(),
});

// Correct: the resource owns a tracked, yieldable request.
query('usersQuery', {
  loader: function* () {
    return yield* CraftHttpClient.get(({ response }) => ({
      url: '/api/users',
      success: response<User[]>(),
    }));
  },
});

no-async-await rejects async, await, and for await...of in Craft code. require-generator-resource-loader additionally checks that query, mutation, and asyncProcess loaders are generators. Use yield* for Craft operations so every suspension stays tracked.

The loader signature should also stay inferred:

ts
// Incorrect: these annotations can mask a mismatch in the resource contract.
loader: function* ({ params }: { params: string }): Generator<Yielded, Result, unknown> {
  return yield* client({ token: params });
}

// Correct: infer params and the generator result from the resource and body.
loader: function* ({ params }) {
  return yield* client({ token: params });
}

no-explicit-resource-loader-type reports only annotations on the loader signature. Type annotations for local variables and function contracts outside the loader remain allowed.

Keep transport and types honest#

ts
// Incorrect: direct fetch bypasses Craft response/error tracking.
const result = await fetch('/api/users');

// Correct: use the Craft client in the owning resource loader.
return (
  yield *
  CraftHttpClient.get(({ response }) => ({
    url: '/api/users',
    success: response<User>(),
  }))
);

For a raw binary body, use CraftBinaryHttpClient.put(...); do not use a type assertion to force CraftHttpClient to accept a Blob. An assertion only silences TypeScript — it does not change the runtime value or transport. That is why prefer-craft-http-transport and no-type-assertions-in-resource-loader report these patterns.

Preserve primitive inference#

The insertion callback already receives a contextual type, and the primitive already knows the complete type of its generator. Do not repeat either type at the boundary:

ts
// ❌ craft-ts/no-explicit-craft-insertion-type
insertQueryPipe(
  ({ resource }): SpaceQueryView => ({
    items: craftUse(craftComputed('items', () => resource.value())),
  }),
);

// ❌ craft-ts/no-craft-primitive-type-assertion
const generator = query('spaceItems', config) as unknown as Generator<
  unknown,
  SpaceQueryRef,
  unknown
>;

// ✅
const generator = query(
  'spaceItems',
  config,
  insertQueryPipe(({ resource }) => ({
    items: craftUse(craftComputed('items', () => resource.value())),
  })),
);

The assertion is especially harmful around a composed insertion pipe: it replaces the type that carries the derived properties and their dependencies.

Prefer primitive deep-yieldable insertions#

When a property is read from the result of a primitive, expose the deep view at the primitive boundary. This keeps the property reader connected to the primitive and avoids an extra adapter:

ts
// ❌ craft-ts/prefer-insert-deep-yieldable
const spaceQuery = yield * spaceQueryGenerator;
const deepItems = deepYieldable(spaceQuery.items);

// ✅ add insertDeepYieldable() to the query call, then:
const spaceQuery = yield * spaceQueryGenerator;
const items = spaceQuery.items;

Expected failures should use craftException(...) so they remain typed and available through the resource's exception state. no-throw keeps technical throws limited to explicit adapter boundaries, where they can be translated into the Craft exception channel.

Accessibility (craft-ts/a11y)#

Spread craftRules.configs.a11y.rules to enable the WCAG 2.2 AA preset as error. The rules walk all hyperscript in the file (craftTemplate, extracted factories, h('tag')), not only craftComponent argument 3.

  • prefer-named-html-helpers: forbids h('img') / h('button') when a named helper exists

  • require-interactive-local-name: requires a string-literal first argument on interactive helpers; the local name is the third segment of data-craft-name="${component}:${tag}:${localName}"

  • img-has-alt, iframe-has-title, button-has-type, anchor-has-href

  • control-has-accessible-name, label-has-associated-control, heading-has-content — a label is associated with any HTML labelable element (button, input other than hidden, meter, output, progress, select, textarea) it wraps or targets with htmlFor, and its text names that control:

    ts
    // ❌ a div is not labelable, even with role=switch
label([span('Dark mode'), div({ role: 'switch', 'aria-checked': 'false' })]);
// ✅ the wrapping label associates and names the native button
label([
  span('Dark mode'),
  button({ type: 'button', role: 'switch', 'aria-checked': 'false' }),
]);

    See Labels and labelable controls.

  • no-noninteractive-element-interactions, no-positive-tabindex

  • valid-aria, role-has-required-aria, target-blank-noopener

  • prefer-relative-heading, require-route-heading-outline, require-outlet-heading-section, no-heading-level-skip

See Accessibility.

The two migration rules also expose a VS Code ESLint Quick Fix suggestion that inserts a temporary local disable comment with the intended migration note when you need to unblock a file before doing the full refactor.

The template and reactivity rules are intentionally diagnostic-only: replacing a resource or subscription can change lifecycle and error semantics, so the rule points at the Craft primitive without applying a potentially unsafe rewrite.

Why templates use blocks#

Craft template blocks preserve the branch structure in the type-level render contract. A ternary or condition && node produces only a computed value, so the type checker cannot assert which branch renders which content. Keep derived values and business decisions in the component's state/query layer, then make the template express visibility explicitly:

ts
ifNode(
  isReady,
  () => p('Ready'),
  () => p('Loading…'),
);

matchNode.exhaustive(query.exceptions, '_tag', {
  NOT_FOUND: () => p('Not found'),
  FORBIDDEN: () => p('Forbidden'),
});

This rule is for Craft's TypeScript templates. It does not rewrite external template languages.

The same restriction applies to boolean expressions. A negation is still application logic, even when it is used only for a DOM property:

ts
// Incorrect: the template derives the disabled state.
button(
  {
    disabled: function* () {
      return !(yield* machine.canGoBack());
    },
  },
